headline: The Medical Receptionist Foundation
threshold: By Lesson 10, you can greet patients, give appointment times and copay amounts, ask for an ID and insurance card, direct patients around the clinic, make polite requests, ask for help, and start Medical Receptionist Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Greet patients at the front desk and say clinic words with clear Spanish vowels and sounds.
lessons.focus: The five vowels, ch, j, ll, rr and written accents; greetings with usted

words.note: In Latin America, c before e or i sounds like s: SI-ta.
The accent marks the stressed syllable: re-cep-CIÓN.
Stress the accented syllable: te-LÉ-fo-no.
Stress the first syllable: CLÍ-ni-ca.
ch sounds like the ch in English 'check'.
j sounds like a strong English h: O-ha. The h is silent.
ll sounds like English y: SI-ya.
rr is a rolled, trilled r.
Say la doctora for a woman and el doctor for a man.
Use from noon until dark; after dark say buenas noches.
Spanish vowels a, e, i, o, u are short and pure. Use usted with patients.

words.en: My name is Ana and I work at the front desk.
words.es: Me llamo Ana y trabajo en la recepción.

words.note: Say señor to a man and señorita to a young woman.

words.es: Hasta luego, que le vaya bien.

lessons.speaking: Greet a patient at the front desk, say your name and that you work there, and ask how they are.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Say appointment times, dates, phone numbers and copay amounts in dollars.
lessons.focus: Numbers 0 to 1,000, clock time with a las, dates, minutes and dollar amounts

words.note: ¿Qué hora es? asks the time on the clock.
Say phone numbers in pairs or one digit at a time.
Days are not capitalized: el lunes, el martes.
Use a las for clock time, but a la 1 for one o'clock.

words.en: The copay is 25 dollars, according to your insurance.
words.es: El copago es de 25 dólares, según su seguro.

words.en: Your date of birth is May 3, 1985.
words.es: Su fecha de nacimiento es el 3 de mayo de 1985.
words.note: Spanish puts the day before the month.

words.en: We open at 8 and close at 5.
words.es: Abrimos a las 8 y cerramos a las 5.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient the appointment day and time, and how many minutes the wait is.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Say who people are and where things are, and describe the clinic as open, busy or ready.
lessons.focus: ser for what something is, estar for its condition or location

words.note: A male nurse is el enfermero.
Agrees with the noun: la clínica está abierta.
Paciente nuevo for a man, paciente nueva for a woman.

words.en: The doctor is busy right now.
words.note: estar for a condition; ocupada agrees with la doctora.

words.es: Soy la recepcionista de la clínica.
words.note: ser for who you are; a man says soy el recepcionista.

words.en: The restroom is on the right.
words.es: El baño está a la derecha.
words.note: estar for location.

words.en: The clinic is closed on Sundays.
words.es: La clínica está cerrada los domingos.
El doctor García es su médico.

words.en: The waiting room is full today.
words.es: La sala de espera está llena hoy.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient where the restroom and waiting room are and whether the doctor is busy or ready.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Say what a patient has, needs or wants, and what must be done at check-in.
lessons.focus: tener, hay, necesitar, querer and hay que + infinitive

words.note: Also heard as la ID in US clinics.
Common in Mexico and the US; also el bolígrafo.

words.en: This form needs to be filled out.
words.note: hay que + infinitive: something must be done, with no specific person.

words.en: There are chairs in the waiting room.
words.es: Hay sillas en la sala de espera.
words.note: hay means both there is and there are.

words.en: Do you have your insurance card?

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient for an ID and insurance card, and say what they need to fill out and sign.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Tell patients where to go, what you are going to do, and when the doctor can see them.
lessons.focus: ir, ir a + infinitive for plans, hacer and poder

words.note: Common in Mexico and the US; Spain says el ascensor.

words.en: I'm going to call the nurse.
words.es: Voy a llamar a la enfermera.
words.note: Use the personal a before a person: llamar a la enfermera.

words.en: You can go to the lab on the second floor.
words.es: Puede ir al laboratorio en el segundo piso.
words.note: a + el becomes al.

words.en: I'm going to make your appointment for Tuesday.
words.es: Voy a hacer su cita para el martes.

words.en: The doctor can see you today at 3.
words.es: La doctora puede verla hoy a las 3.
words.note: verla for a woman, verlo for a man.

words.en: First you go to the lab and then to the pharmacy.
words.es: Primero va al laboratorio y luego a la farmacia.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient where to go next, the lab or the pharmacy, and when the doctor can see them.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Describe daily front-desk actions with regular present-tense verbs.
lessons.focus: Present tense -ar, -er, -ir verbs for yo, tú, usted, nosotros, ellos

words.note: Many Latino patients have two last names; ask for both.
A man is el recepcionista.

words.en: I arrive at the clinic at 7:30.
words.es: Llego a la clínica a las 7:30.
words.note: -ar verbs, yo: llego, llamo, espero.

words.en: Do you live at this address?
words.note: -ir verbs, usted: vive, escribe, abre.

words.en: I type your first and last name into the computer.
words.es: Escribo su nombre y apellido en la computadora.
Nosotros abrimos la ventanilla a las 8.

words.en: They wait in the waiting room.
words.es: Ellos esperan en la sala de espera.

words.en: Do you read the phone messages?
words.note: Informal tú is for coworkers; use usted with patients.

lessons.speaking: Tell a coworker about your day at the desk: when you arrive, when you open the window and who reads the messages.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask patients basic questions about their name, birth date, doctor and insurance.
lessons.focus: Question words qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué, cuál

words.note: Agrees with the noun: ¿cuántos minutos?, ¿cuántas páginas?
¿Cómo? alone also means 'Sorry, what did you say?'
Two words with an accent asks why; porque (one word) means because.
Use ¿cuál es...? to ask for data: name, number, date.

words.en: What is your date of birth?
When do you want to come in?
Why do you need to see the doctor?
words.note: Personal a before a person: ver al médico.

words.en: How do you spell your last name?

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient their date of birth, who their doctor is and what insurance they have, and write down the answers.

lessons.title: No, Never and How Much
lessons.objective: Say no, nobody, nothing and not yet, and talk about more, less and another at the desk.
lessons.focus: no, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no, más, menos, otro

words.note: Never say un otro: say otro formulario, otra cita.

words.en: There's no one in the restroom.
words.es: No hay nadie en el baño.
words.note: Spanish uses a double negative: no hay nadie.

words.es: La doctora todavía no está lista.

words.en: There are fewer patients in the afternoon.
words.es: Hay menos pacientes en la tarde.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient the doctor isn't ready yet, how many more minutes to wait, and that nobody is ahead of them.

lessons.title: Polite Requests and Commands
lessons.objective: Ask patients politely to sit, sign, wait or repeat with ¿Puede…? and usted commands.
lessons.focus: ¿Puede…? + infinitive and usted commands for everyday verbs

words.note: Common in Mexico and the US; also la mascarilla.
¿Puede + infinitive? is the softest way to ask.
Usted command: tomar becomes tome.

words.en: Please hold the line for a moment.
words.es: Espere un momento en la línea, por favor.

words.en: Please put on the face mask.
Can you repeat your name, please?
Fill out the first page and sign at the bottom.
words.es: Llene la primera página y firme abajo.

lessons.speaking: Politely ask a patient to have a seat, put on a mask, repeat their name and sign the form.

lessons.title: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objective: Use Spanish words you already know and ask for help when you don't understand.
lessons.focus: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad, -ente and survival phrases

words.note: -ción words are feminine and match English -tion.
-dad words are feminine: la enfermedad.
-ente words: el paciente for a man, la paciente for a woman.
Same form for men and women.
Use el or la to match the person.

words.en: I don't understand, can you speak more slowly?
One moment, I'm going to call an interpreter.
words.es: Un momento, voy a llamar a un intérprete.

words.en: How do you say 'copay' in Spanish?

words.es: Si es una emergencia, llame al 911.

words.en: I need help at the front desk, please.
words.es: Necesito ayuda en la recepción, por favor.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient you speak a little Spanish, ask them to speak more slowly, and say you will call an interpreter.
